analysis.one_liner: Strips the National Labor Relations Board of its power to prosecute unfair labor practices and issue workplace rules.
analysis.headline: A bill to overhaul federal labor law enforcement was introduced with 72 Republican cosponsors, but the House committee with jurisdiction never held a markup or vote, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would take away the National Labor Relations Board's power to issue complaints and prosecute employers or unions for unfair labor practices, and take away its power to stop such practices. Instead, a worker or union that says its rights were violated would have to file a lawsuit in federal court and pay for the litigation itself. It would also stop the Board from writing any rules that affect the rights of workers, employers, or unions, limiting it to running its own internal operations.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers accused of unfair labor practices, such as firing workers for organizing or refusing to bargain, would no longer face prosecution by the National Labor Relations Board, which pursues those cases at no cost to the worker. Disputes would shift to private federal lawsuits, which favor parties who can afford lawyers. The bill also ends Board rulemaking on substantive rights, so employers would no longer face new workplace rules written by the Board.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the General Counsel's authority to issue complaints charging unfair labor practices and to prosecute them before the Board, and repeals the Board's power to prevent a person from engaging in an unfair labor practice.
Limits Board rulemaking to rules about the Board's internal functions and prohibits any rules affecting the substantive rights of any person, employer, employee, or labor organization.
Allows an aggrieved party to bring a civil action, including for injunctions, in federal district court when a person has engaged in or is about to engage in an unfair labor practice.
Requires the Board, within six months of enactment, to review and revise all existing regulations to implement the changes.

analysis.who_pays: Workers and unions would lose the free government enforcement machinery they rely on to challenge unlawful firings, retaliation, and refusal to bargain. Enforcing labor rights would become a private lawsuit, meaning workers would bear the cost of litigation and face employers with far more resources. Supporters argued the change restores a fairer process by moving cases out of a system where the agency both prosecutes and judges them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers and unions enforcing labor rights

drawbacks.text: Workers would have to pay for their own federal lawsuits to enforce rights the Board currently enforces at no cost to them, a system that favors well-resourced employers over individual workers.
The bill repeals the Board's power to prevent unfair labor practices, so there would be no government mechanism to stop ongoing violations, only after-the-fact litigation.

The strongest good-faith case for the bill is that the Board currently writes rules with the force of law and prosecutes cases before administrative judges inside the same agency, which supporters viewed as unchecked agency power; this bill addresses that by limiting rulemaking and moving disputes to federal court, but at the price of the enforcement system workers currently use.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill mainly benefits employers by dismantling the government's mechanism for prosecuting unfair labor practices and by blocking Board rulemaking on substantive rights. Its main cost falls on workers and unions, who would have to litigate violations themselves in federal court. Even on its own terms, the replacement system is tilted toward parties who can afford sustained litigation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee for the rest of the Congress — it was referred to the full committee and then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Austin Scott (R-GA) introduced the bill on April 17, 2015, joined by 18 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced.
On November 16, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, and no further action was taken.
The bill had 72 cosponsors, all Republicans.
The Congress ended January 3, 2017, with the bill never brought to a vote in committee or on the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained ground — workers kept the existing National Labor Relations Board enforcement system, and employers who would have benefited from the changes did not get them. The bill's sponsor and cosponsors made their position part of the record without changing any law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers; labor law enforcement stayed unchanged

for.name: 72 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.

sides.party_line_note: All 72 cosponsors, including the sponsor, were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the bill never reached a floor vote where party splits would be recorded.

industries.industry: Employers, especially those facing union organizing or labor disputes
